articles.title: The Weekly Variance Conversation
articles.dek: How one structured meeting turns food cost from a surprise into a system.
articles.body: Most restaurants review food cost monthly, which means problems compound for weeks before anyone sees them. The weekly variance conversation changes this. Every week, the manager pulls beginning inventory, purchases, and ending inventory. They calculate actual food cost percentage and compare it to the budget target. The meeting is not the owner asking what happened. The meeting is the manager arriving with three things: the number, the cause, and the fix. When a manager arrives with the actual result, the target, the identified cause, and a par-level correction already underway, the conversation operates at a different level. The owner's role shifts from interrogator to coach. This structure works because it is weekly, because the manager owns the number, and because the corrective action happens before the next period begins. The variance conversation is not a report. It is a discipline.
takeaways: Calculate actual food cost every week, not monthly
The manager presents the number, the cause, and the corrective action
Weekly cadence prevents problems from compounding across periods
articles.sourceNote: Adapted from David Scott Peters weekly food cost methodology

articles.title: The Shift Handoff That Actually Works
articles.dek: A five-minute structure that prevents the two most common service failures.
articles.body: The two most common service failures happen at shift transitions: information that was known by the outgoing manager is lost, and problems that started on one shift become invisible on the next. A structured shift handoff prevents both. The outgoing manager writes three things before leaving: what is working, what needs attention, and any guest or staff issues in progress. The incoming manager reads it, asks one clarifying question, and acknowledges. This takes five minutes. The handoff is not a novel. It is three short statements written on a consistent template. The intended outcome is fewer dropped reservations, fewer repeated guest issues, and stronger continuity between services. The format matters less than the consistency. Whether it is a notebook, a shared document, or a whiteboard, the discipline is the same: do not leave the building without handing off the shift.
takeaways: Write three things: what is working, what needs attention, what is in progress
Incoming manager reads and acknowledges before taking the floor
Consistency of the practice matters more than the format
articles.sourceNote: Common restaurant operating practice, referenced in DSP management systems

articles.title: The Scheduling Trap That Costs You Every Week
articles.dek: Why filling shifts is not the same as scheduling on budget.
articles.body: Most managers schedule by filling shifts. They look at who is available, plug people in, and publish. The problem is that this approach has no financial target. You discover whether you were over budget after payroll runs, which is too late to fix. Scheduling on budget means starting with a labor cost target for the week, calculated from projected sales. The manager builds the schedule against that target, seeing projected hours and dollars before publishing. If Thursday dinner is projected over its labor target, the adjustment happens before the schedule goes live, not after the payroll report. The shift from reactive to proactive scheduling requires two things: a sales forecast and scheduling software that shows labor dollars alongside hours. Without both, the manager is guessing. With both, the manager is managing. This is the difference between a schedule that fills shifts and a schedule that controls cost.
takeaways: Start with a weekly labor cost target derived from projected sales
See projected hours and dollars before publishing the schedule
Adjust before the schedule goes live, not after payroll runs
articles.sourceNote: Based on David Scott Peters Restaurant Payroll Guardian framework

articles.title: Why the Manager Log Is the Most Underused Tool in Restaurants
articles.dek: A daily log that turns scattered observations into operational memory.
articles.body: Every restaurant has managers who notice things during a shift: a prep issue, a guest complaint pattern, a piece of equipment acting up, a server who needs coaching. Most of this information lives in the manager's head and disappears when they leave for the night. The manager log captures it. A simple daily entry that records what happened, what was resolved, and what needs follow-up. The log is not a diary. It is operational memory. When a pattern appears across three entries, it becomes visible as a system problem rather than an isolated incident. When a new manager reads the past week of logs, they inherit context instead of starting blind. The log also creates accountability. If a manager writes that the walk-in temperature was high on Tuesday and no one follows up by Wednesday, the log makes the gap visible. The operating objective is to surface recurring problems earlier and strengthen handoffs between managers.
takeaways: Record what happened, what was resolved, and what needs follow-up daily
Patterns across entries reveal system problems, not just incidents
New managers inherit operational context instead of starting without it

articles.title: Ideal vs. Actual: The Report That Finds Your Money
articles.dek: How to use POS data and inventory to find where product disappears.
articles.body: The ideal vs. actual product usage report compares two numbers: what you should have used based on what the POS says you sold, and what you actually used based on inventory counts. The gap between these two numbers tells you where product is disappearing. If the POS says you sold 40 orders of salmon this week, and your recipe card says each order uses 7 ounces, the ideal usage is 280 ounces. If your inventory shows you actually used 340 ounces, that 60-ounce gap represents waste, portioning errors, unreported spoilage, or theft. Without this report, you know your food cost is high but you do not know why. With this report, you can identify exactly which products are over-used and investigate the cause. The report requires three inputs: accurate recipe costing cards, reliable POS data, and consistent inventory counts. If any of these inputs is unreliable, the report will be misleading. This is why recipe cards and inventory discipline must come first. The ideal vs. actual report is the payoff for building those foundational systems.
takeaways: Compare what the POS says you sold against what inventory says you used
The gap identifies specific products with waste, portioning, or loss issues
Requires accurate recipe cards, POS data, and inventory counts to be useful
articles.sourceNote: Based on David Scott Peters food management software methodology

articles.title: Table Touching Is a Management Skill, Not a Personality Trait
articles.dek: How structured floor presence builds guest loyalty and staff accountability.
articles.body: Some managers touch tables naturally. Most do not, and the ones who avoid it often believe it is a personality trait rather than a skill. Table touching is a management skill that can be structured and practiced. The manager's presence on the floor during service serves two purposes: it builds direct relationships with guests, and it provides real-time oversight of service execution. When guests begin asking for a manager by name rather than just the owner, that is a signal that the culture is working. The practice is simple: during peak service, the manager visits every table in their section. Not to sell, not to apologize, but to connect. A brief check-in, a genuine question about the meal, and an acknowledgment. The discipline is doing it every shift, not just when things go wrong. Managers who practice structured table touching also catch service problems earlier, because they see what is happening at the table level instead of from behind the host stand.
takeaways: Table touching is a structured skill, not a personality trait
Visit every table during peak service for brief, genuine check-ins
Consistent floor presence catches service problems earlier
articles.sourceNote: Adapted from David Scott Peters guest relationship methodology
